articles.role: Explanatory articles written for the cover animation, based on the existing case research. These are not separate news reports, original article excerpts, model outputs or new occurrence records.
articles.source: Castro et al. (2024), Large language models overcome the challenges of unstructured text data in ecology, Ecological Informatics 82:102742, Table 2 and the existing case source notes.
articles.exampleRole: The English hornet sentence is an explanatory adaptation of the Table 2 example recorded in the case notes, not a verified verbatim quotation from the original news item.

articles.headline: A hornet appears in a report
paragraphs: A short report can contain a useful clue about an animal's whereabouts. The study's Jersey example can be adapted as a simple sentence: An invasive hornet was found on Jersey for the first time. That sentence brings an animal, a place and a statement of discovery into the same passage.

The task is to decide whether the passage supports a record of occurrence. Finding the word hornet is only the beginning. The reader must connect the animal to what happened and where it happened. A place mentioned elsewhere in an article might have a different role in the story.

A record drawn from this example should remain attached to its original source text. The paper supplies an expected interpretation of the passage, rather than a new observation made for this website. Before using a report in research, someone must check whether its wording and geographic detail support the proposed record.

articles.headline: Finding the place in a paragraph
paragraphs: A place name gives a reader somewhere to start, but its role depends on the sentence around it. In the Jersey example, the place belongs to the statement that a hornet was found. The text supports a reported region. It does not supply the exact spot where someone saw the insect.

Other passages can use a place name differently. A text might mention a researcher's workplace, describe a comparison, or discuss an area where a species could live. These are reading examples, not additional reports from the study. The question is whether the passage links the named place to an occurrence.

A map should preserve that level of detail. If a report names an island, the map can show the island as the reported area. Choosing a coordinate inside it does not recover a missing observation site. The geographic information remains regional, even when the coordinate is written with many decimal places.

articles.headline: Suitable habitat is a different claim
paragraphs: Consider a teaching example that says Jersey could provide suitable conditions for a hornet in the future. It contains the same animal and place as a report of discovery. Yet the claim is different. It describes a possibility, without saying that the animal has already been found in that area.

A search for names alone would miss this distinction. The meaning lies in how the words work together. Could live, was found and might arrive do not make the same statement. A reader must establish which claim the text actually makes before turning a passage into a candidate occurrence record.

The distinction also needs care in the other direction. A passage can support an occurrence without using the exact phrase was found. The paper includes indirect descriptions that count as positive examples. Reading the full context is more useful than treating every indirect mention as evidence that no occurrence was reported.

articles.headline: Reading beyond the species name
paragraphs: In this study, the target species is specified before the text is examined. The model is asked to read about that species and decide what the passage supports. It is not identifying the insect from a photograph. The hornet shown in this animation introduces the subject, while the written passage carries the occurrence clue.

The surrounding sentences matter because an animal's name can appear in a discussion without describing a local observation. A paragraph may compare claims or explain what could happen. Those possibilities are examples of reading problems, not extra findings. The reader needs to identify the statement made about the animal in that passage.

Keeping the words together helps avoid a tempting shortcut: extracting a species name and a place, then assuming they form a record. Their relationship has to come from the text. A candidate record should express that relationship clearly enough for another person to return to the passage and examine the same interpretation.

articles.headline: Turning a passage into a record
paragraphs: Once a passage supports an occurrence, its information can be arranged for review. The Jersey example in the paper has an expected positive answer and an expected place name. These fields refer back to the same supplied passage. They do not represent a new model run or a fresh field observation made for this animation.

The useful change is one of organisation. A reader can inspect the reported animal and region without losing the sentence that supports them. Unclear details should remain unclear. A neat table cannot supply a missing observation site, resolve an uncertain claim, or establish a date that the available source does not provide.

Moving these fields onto a map makes the geographic relationship easier to see. It should not make the evidence appear more precise than it is. Here the map locates a reported region, while the hornet provides a visual cue to the subject. The two belong to an explanation of the text.

articles.headline: Keeping the source beside the map
paragraphs: A map is easier to read than a pile of passages, but it leaves much of their context out of sight. Keeping the source beside a candidate record lets someone check what was said. That review concerns the wording and its support for a record; it does not replace confirmation in the field.

Time also needs careful reading. A statement that an animal was found for the first time does not establish when it first arrived. The discovery described by a report and the animal's earlier history are different questions. This animation supplies no new observation date, arrival date or account of movement across the map.

The papers that gather into the world map are explanatory texts written for this cover. They are not a collection of newly verified news reports. Their movement shows how scattered writing can be organised into geographic clues. The final Jersey example retains a regional meaning, with the source and its limits still visible.
